36.title: A king with no sons
36.howItsDone: Many Hindus read the Ramayana in their own language, recite it at home or in temples, and watch it performed as Ramlila each autumn; Rama's birthday is celebrated as Rama Navami in spring.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sankat mochan, and a mountain carried through the night. Your line was bring the whole mountain. You've met Hanuman. Now for five weeks, the whole story he lives inside. Day thirty-six.

Ayodhya. A shining city on a river, walls and gardens and elephants, and a good king named Dasharatha. His name means ten chariots: a man who could drive in every direction at once. He has everything. Wealth. Peace. Three queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And no children. Year after year after year. The kingdom waits for an heir. The king grows old. He has done everything a king can do, and the one thing he wants most has not come. You probably know someone like him. Maybe you are someone like him. The thing everyone else seems to get easily just keeps not arriving.

This is the opening of the Ramayana, the story of Rama. Tradition says it was composed by Valmiki, called the first poet: about twenty-four thousand verses in seven books. For many Hindus it's not just a story but scripture, and every Indian language has its own retellings. For the next five weeks we'll walk through it, one scene a day, like a serial. Here's how it starts. Dasharatha's advisers suggest a great sacrifice, a fire ritual for the sake of sons. They bring a young sage, Rishyashringa, to lead it. The fire is lit. The offerings go in. And out of the flames rises a shining figure, carrying a golden bowl filled with sweet rice pudding, payasa, sent by the gods. Give this to your queens, he says. Dasharatha divides it among the three. And in time, four sons are born. Kausalya bears Rama. Kaikeyi bears Bharata. Sumitra bears twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Four boys, after all those years. The text also says something the gods are doing behind the scenes: Vishnu, the preserver, has chosen to be born as Rama to deal with a demon king no god can defeat. Remember that, and remember the name Kaikeyi. Here's what the story knows. The greatest story in the tradition begins with a long wait. Not a battle. Not a hero. An old man hoping. And the answer, when it comes, is bigger than what he asked for. He wanted one heir. He got four sons, and one of them changes everything. Some things arrive late.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a wish that's taking too long. Settle, and breathe. Name something you've been waiting for. A job, a healing, a person, a child, a change. Don't pretend it doesn't hurt. Let the wanting be there. Then breathe with it, without asking it to hurry. If you pray, you can hold it up to God. If you don't, just hold it gently, like a bowl. The bell holds the time.
A king with no sons. Dasharatha waits for years, a fire ritual brings a golden bowl, and four sons are born: Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana and Shatrughna.

segments.voice: Your line: some things arrive late. Today, be patient with one thing that's slower than you want. Day thirty-six.

37.title: Rama grows up
37.hook: the four brothers; the bow no one can lift
37.howItsDone: Rama's youth, his journey with Vishvamitra and the lifting of Shiva's bow are favorite scenes in Ramlila plays and in children's retellings of the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king with no sons, and four boys born after the long wait. Your line was some things arrive late. Today, the boys grow up, and one of them is asked to leave home. Day thirty-seven.

Four brothers growing up in a palace. Rama and Lakshmana are inseparable; Bharata and Shatrughna are too. They learn the scriptures, archery, riding, how to rule. Then one day a famous sage walks into the court. Vishvamitra. Demons keep ruining his sacrifices in the forest, and he wants help. Not the army. Not the king. He wants Rama. Who is, the text says, not yet sixteen. Dasharatha, who waited half his life for this boy, panics. Take my army, take me, he says, just not my son. And the family priest, Vasishtha, gently tells the king: let him go. He'll be safe with this teacher. And he'll need what he learns.
screen: `FOUR BROTHERS.` → `THE SAGE WANTS RAMA.` → `NOT YET SIXTEEN.` → `LET HIM GO.`

segments.voice: So Rama and Lakshmana walk out into the forest behind the sage. It's their first time away from home. Vishvamitra teaches them divine weapons and mantras as they walk. They guard his sacrifice, and drive the demons off. One of those demons, Maricha, is knocked far across the sea by a single arrow of Rama's and survives. Hold on to his name; he'll be back. Then the sage says: come with me to Mithila. King Janaka has something you should see. In Janaka's court sits a bow that once belonged to Shiva himself. It's so heavy that, in Valmiki's telling, it's wheeled in on an enormous iron cart dragged by thousands of men. Kings and princes and warriors have come from everywhere to try to lift it. Not one of them could so much as bend it. Janaka has made a promise: whoever can string this bow may marry his daughter, Sita. Rama walks up to the bow. The whole court watches. And he lifts it, as if it were nothing. Here's what the story knows. The bow has been sitting there for years, too heavy for everyone. It was waiting for the one person whose weight it was. Not the strongest man in the room in general. The right person, for this particular weight. Most of us have a bow like that. Something in your family, your work, your street, that everyone else walks past, and that somehow fits your hands. That's your weight. Tomorrow: what happens when Rama tries to string it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a thing only you can lift. Sit and breathe. Ask yourself what weight in your life seems shaped for your hands. Something others can't quite carry, or haven't noticed. A relative only you can talk to. A skill. A problem at work nobody else understands. Don't pick it up yet. Just notice it's there, and notice how it feels to think: this one might be mine. The bell holds the time.
Rama grows up. He leaves home with the sage Vishvamitra, learns to fight, and lifts Shiva's bow in Janaka's court when no one else could.
Your line: your weight. Today, lift one thing that everyone else keeps walking past, and see if it fits your hands. Day thirty-seven.

38.title: Sita's swayamvara
38.howItsDone: The wedding of Rama and Sita is celebrated as Vivah Panchami in parts of India and Nepal, especially around Janakpur, and the breaking of the bow is a high point of Ramlila performances.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rama grows up, and lifts the bow no one else could. Your line was your weight. Did something fit your hands? Today, he tries to string it. Day thirty-eight.

First, who is Sita. Years ago, King Janaka was plowing a field for a ritual, and his plow turned up something in the furrow: a baby girl, lying in the earth. He took her home and raised her as his daughter. He named her Sita, which means furrow. A daughter of the earth itself. Now she's grown, and her father has set the test: the man who strings Shiva's bow may marry her. Rama holds the great bow. He bends it. He pulls the string toward its notch. And the bow, which no one else could even move, snaps in half, with a crack like thunder. The text says people in the hall fell to the ground from the sound.
screen: `A BABY IN A FURROW.` → `SITA MEANS FURROW.` → `THE BOW SNAPS.` → `A CRACK LIKE THUNDER.`

segments.voice: Today's title uses the word swayamvara. Swayam means self. Vara means choice, or the chosen groom. Swayamvara: choosing for yourself. It was an old custom in the epics: a princess chooses her husband, often by placing a garland around his neck. Here's where the versions part, and it's worth knowing. In Valmiki's Ramayana, strictly speaking, this isn't a choosing. Janaka had promised Sita as the prize of strength: whoever strings the bow wins her. Rama breaks it, and Janaka gives her to him. But in the Ramcharitmanas, the sixteenth-century retelling by Tulsidas, loved across North India, there's a scene before the contest. Sita walks into a flower garden to pray, and sees Rama there, picking flowers for his teacher. She falls in love on the spot, and prays to the goddess Parvati that he'll be the one. When the bow breaks, she walks forward and puts the victory garland around his neck. She chooses. Both tellings are held dear. Many Hindus picture this scene as Tulsidas tells it; many know Valmiki's version too. And Sita is not a prize in the hearts of the people who love this story. She's a goddess for many of them, Lakshmi herself. Here's what the story knows. Some choices are made in the loud moment, the bow cracking. Some were made quietly, earlier, in a garden, when no one was looking. The garland only says out loud what the heart already chose.
screen: `SWAYAMVARA — CHOOSING FOR YOURSELF.` · `IN VALMIKI: THE PRIZE OF STRENGTH.` · `IN TULSIDAS: THE GARDEN, THE GARLAND.` · `THE HEART CHOSE FIRST.` · then, large: `CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choosing, being chosen. Sit and breathe. Think of a time someone chose you. A friend who picked you, a partner, a team, a teacher who saw something in you. Let yourself feel that. Then think of something you chose: a person, a path, a place. Did you choose it in a loud moment or a quiet one? Let both sit with you, being chosen and choosing. The bell holds the time.
Sita's swayamvara. Rama breaks Shiva's bow, and in the best-loved telling Sita garlands him: her choice, made first in a garden.
Your line: choose. Today, one decision you've been drifting on: make it, out loud, even a small one. Day thirty-eight.

39.title: Kaikeyi's two wishes
39.hook: the maid Manthara; the old promise called in
39.howItsDone: Hindus retell Kaikeyi's wishes as the turning point of the Ramayana; in Ramlila performances it's often the moment the audience goes quiet, and many discuss how much blame Kaikeyi and Manthara bear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita's swayamvara: a bow snapped, a garland placed. Your line was choose. What did you decide? Today, years later, back in Ayodhya, a happy announcement goes wrong overnight. Day thirty-nine.

Dasharatha is old now, and he makes the announcement the whole kingdom wants: tomorrow, Rama will be crowned as heir. The city goes wild. Flags, flowers, lamps in every window. And in the palace, Queen Kaikeyi, Bharata's mother, hears the news and is delighted. She loves Rama. She even gives a jewel to the servant who brought the news. That servant is her old maid, Manthara, who came with her from her childhood home. And Manthara throws the jewel down. Are you a fool, she says. When Rama is king, his mother will be queen mother, and you'll be her servant. And your son, Bharata, will have nothing.
screen: `TOMORROW, RAMA WILL BE CROWNED.` → `KAIKEYI IS DELIGHTED.` → `MANTHARA THROWS THE JEWEL DOWN.`

segments.voice: At first Kaikeyi argues. Rama is good. Rama is fair. But Manthara keeps talking, all night, and slowly the fear gets in. Then Manthara reminds her of something. Long ago, in a battle, Dasharatha was wounded, and Kaikeyi saved his life. In gratitude, he promised her two wishes, anything she asked, and she never used them. Use them now. So Kaikeyi goes to the room where a queen goes when she is angry, throws off her jewelry, and lies on the bare floor. Dasharatha finds her there, and he's frantic. What's wrong? I'll give you anything. And she makes him swear it, on Rama's name. Then she asks. First wish: crown Bharata instead. Second wish: send Rama into the forest, in exile, for fourteen years. The old king collapses. He begs. He argues. He pleads all night. But he gave his word, and a king's word is dharma. He can't take it back. Now, who is to blame? The tradition argues. In Valmiki, Kaikeyi and Manthara make a real, human choice. In some later tellings, the gods themselves arrange it: they send the goddess Saraswati to turn Manthara's mind, because Rama has to reach the forest to do what he was born to do. Those tellings are gentler on Kaikeyi. Strip the story down and it's simple. Two wishes, given in a grateful moment years ago, almost forgotten. Then someone picks them up, and they become a weapon. Words have weight. A promise keeps its weight long after the moment you made it.
screen: `MANTHARA TALKS ALL NIGHT.` · `THE OLD PROMISE: TWO WISHES.` · `CROWN BHARATA. EXILE RAMA.` · `WHO IS TO BLAME? IT DEPENDS.` · then, large: `WORDS HAVE WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a promise that trapped you. Sit and breathe. Think of a promise you made easily, that later got heavy. Maybe you're still keeping it. Maybe you broke it. Or think of a voice, like Manthara's, that talked you into something at night that looked different in the morning. No judgment. Just see the weight of the words. Then breathe out, and let them rest. The bell holds the time.
Kaikeyi's two wishes. Old promises called in: Bharata to be crowned, and Rama sent into the forest for fourteen years.
Your line: words have weight. Today, before you promise anything, even something small, weigh it first. Day thirty-nine.

40.title: Fourteen years
40.hook: Rama exiled; he accepts in one sentence
40.howItsDone: Many Hindus hold up Rama's acceptance of exile as the model of keeping one's word and duty; the scene is often retold when families talk about hard decisions and honoring parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kaikeyi's two wishes: Bharata crowned, Rama exiled. Your line was words have weight. Now someone has to tell Rama. It's the morning of his coronation. Day forty.

Rama wakes up on the most important morning of his life. The city is decorated for him. The priests are ready. The water for the ceremony has been gathered from sacred rivers. A messenger comes: your father wants to see you. Rama walks into Kaikeyi's rooms expecting a blessing, and finds his father on the floor, unable to look at him, unable to speak. Kaikeyi speaks instead. Calmly, she tells him everything. Bharata will be king. You will go to the forest, dressed as a hermit, for fourteen years. Your father promised. Everyone in the room waits to see what Rama will do.
screen: `THE CORONATION MORNING.` → `HIS FATHER CAN'T SPEAK.` → `FOURTEEN YEARS IN THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Rama says, in effect: so be it. I'll go. He doesn't argue. He doesn't bargain. He tells Kaikeyi he would have given the kingdom to Bharata gladly if anyone had simply asked. His only sorrow is that his father is in pain. Then he walks out. Valmiki notices one detail, and people have repeated it for two thousand years: Rama's face didn't change. It looked the same when he heard he'd be king, and when he heard he'd be exiled. Now, that isn't coldness. The people around him are anything but calm. His mother Kausalya is devastated. His brother Lakshmana is furious and ready to fight their father for the throne. Rama is the steady one, and he talks Lakshmana down. Why does he accept? Because of dharma, your third word: doing what's yours to do. For Rama, keeping his father's word is his duty, even when it costs him everything. For many Hindus that's why he's called maryada purushottam: the ideal person, who keeps within the bounds of right action. Not everyone finds this easy. Readers have always asked whether Rama should have fought, and the tradition lets people ask. But here's what the story knows. There is a difference between giving up and accepting. Giving up sits down. Accepting stands up and starts walking. Rama doesn't pretend it's fair. He just refuses to let the unfairness decide who he is. The Gita's line is hiding here too: the action is yours, the fruit isn't. Accept, then walk.
screen: `SO BE IT. I'LL GO.` · `HIS FACE DIDN'T CHANGE.` · `DHARMA: KEEP THE FATHER'S WORD.` · `ACCEPTING ISN'T GIVING UP.` · then, large: `ACCEPT, THEN WALK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with an unfair sentence, calmly. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that isn't fair and won't change. A diagnosis, a loss, a decision someone else made. Don't argue with it for these two minutes. Let your face be still, the way Rama's was. Breathe in: this is what is. Breathe out: what's my next step? The bell holds the time.
Fourteen years. Rama's exile, accepted in a sentence, on the morning he was meant to be crowned.
Your line: accept, then walk. Today, when something unfair lands, give it one breath, then take the next step anyway. Day forty.

41.title: Sita insists
41.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Sita as a model of loyalty and strength; her insistence on going into exile is retold at weddings, in Ramlila, and in women's songs across India.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fourteen years: Rama accepted exile in a sentence. Your line was accept, then walk. Now he goes to tell his wife, and he expects her to stay. Day forty-one.

Rama finds Sita in their rooms, still dressed for the coronation. He tells her. Then he tells her what he's decided for her: you'll stay here, in the palace, where you're safe. Honor my father. Be kind to Bharata. Wait for me. And he describes the forest, to make sure she understands. Thorns on the paths. Lions and snakes. Cold nights on the bare ground. Hunger. Heat. Wind. It's no place for a princess. He thinks he's protecting her. He thinks the conversation is over. It isn't.
screen: `STAY HERE, WHERE IT'S SAFE.` → `THORNS, LIONS, COLD, HUNGER.` → `HE THINKS IT'S OVER.`

segments.voice: Sita answers, and in Valmiki's Ramayana she doesn't answer quietly. She tells him that a wife shares her husband's fortune, whatever it is. If you're going into the forest today, she says, I'll go ahead of you, and walk down the thorns and the sharp grass so your path is softer. With you, the forest is a palace. Without you, the palace is nothing. He keeps refusing. So she gets sharper. She asks, in effect, whether her father married her to a man who only looks like a man, if he'll leave his wife behind out of fear. She weeps. She says if he leaves her, she won't live. And Rama gives in. She comes. Here's what the story knows. Sita isn't following orders. She's overruling them. The prince who calmly accepted exile from his father can't win an argument with his wife. The tradition calls a wife sahadharmini: the one who shares dharma. Sita takes that literally. His path is her path, and she won't let him walk it alone. People read this scene in more than one way. Many see it as the model of devotion in marriage. Others hear, especially in that sharp line, a woman with her own will, choosing her own life, right after we saw her choose her husband. Both readings live in the tradition. Neighbors know a line like this too: Ruth, in the Hebrew Bible, tells her mother-in-law, where you go, I will go. Some loyalty sounds the same in every language. Where you go.
screen: `I'LL WALK AHEAD, ON THE THORNS.` · `WITH YOU, THE FOREST IS A PALACE.` · `SHE OVERRULES HIM.` · `SAHADHARMINI: SHARING DHARMA.` · then, large: `WHERE YOU GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: loyalty you'd walk into a forest for. Sit and breathe. Who would you follow into hard places? A partner, a sibling, a friend, a child. Picture them. Then ask the harder question: who would walk into a forest for you? Let their face come. Just sit with both, the loyalty you give and the loyalty you're given. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Sita insists. Told to stay safe in the palace, she argues her way into exile beside Rama: his path is hers.
Your line: where you go. Today, tell one person, in your own words, that you're with them, whatever path they're on. Day forty-one.

42.title: Lakshmana follows
42.howItsDone: In many Hindu temples and home shrines, Rama is shown with Sita on one side and Lakshmana on the other, often with Hanuman kneeling before them; Lakshmana is honored as the model of a devoted brother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita insists, and argues her way into the forest. Your line was where you go. Two are going now. Today, a third, and the end of the week. Day forty-two.

Nobody asked Lakshmana to go. Nobody exiled him. He could stay in the palace, a prince, with his own wife, Urmila, and a comfortable life, for fourteen years. Rama even tells him to stay: look after our mothers, look after the kingdom. And Lakshmana falls at his brother's feet and says no. Since they were boys, the two have been inseparable. The text says, from childhood, Rama couldn't sleep unless Lakshmana was beside him, couldn't eat unless he ate too. So Lakshmana says: I'll go ahead of you with a bow. I'll dig for roots and gather fruit. I'll keep watch while you and Sita sleep. Just don't leave me here.
screen: `NOBODY EXILED HIM.` → `STAY, RAMA SAYS.` → `I'LL KEEP WATCH WHILE YOU SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Then Lakshmana goes to say goodbye to his own mother, Sumitra. And she gives him one of the most loved blessings in the whole Ramayana. In Valmiki's words, roughly: think of Rama as your father, Dasharatha. Think of Sita as me, your mother. Think of the forest as Ayodhya, your home. Now go, my son. Three sentences, and everything is rearranged. Home is wherever these people are. So the three of them leave, together, walking out of the city while the people run after the chariot, weeping. Here's what the story knows. Rama is the hero. Sita is the heart. And Lakshmana is the third, the one who carries the bags, builds the hut, stays awake. Without the third, the other two don't make it. Most stories forget the third. This one keeps him beside the hero in every picture, and many temples place his image right there with Rama and Sita. And the story is honest about the cost. Lakshmana leaves his wife, Urmila, behind for fourteen years. Valmiki says almost nothing about her. Later tellings filled the silence: in one well-known folk version, she sleeps for fourteen years so her husband can stay awake. The old text is silent; people wanted her remembered anyway. Now look back at this week. A king waited for sons. A boy lifted a bow no one else could. A bow broke and a garland was placed. Two wishes turned into a sentence. A prince accepted it in one breath. A wife refused to stay behind. And a brother nobody asked to go, went anyway.
screen: `THINK OF THE FOREST AS AYODHYA.` · `THE ONE WHO STAYS AWAKE.` · `URMILA, LEFT BEHIND.` · `A WEEK OF THE RAMAYANA.` · then, large: `THE THIRD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the person who'd follow you. Sit and breathe. Think of your third: the one who shows up without being asked. Who carries the bags, drives you to the airport, stays on the phone. Picture them clearly. Then think of someone for whom you are the third. Hold both. And spare a thought for the Urmilas, the people who stay behind so someone else can go. The bell holds the time.
Lakshmana follows. Rama's brother goes into exile unasked, with his mother's blessing: the forest will be your home.
Your line: the third. Today, thank your third, the one who shows up unasked, or be someone's. Day forty-two.
